title: Why 35% growth is boring: the tedious price of Buffett-style steady growth and profitability
summary: Sam reflects on Warren Buffett's time on the Washington Post board, where revenue grew a steady 12% a year and profitability surged but the company became stodgy. He argues that building a Buffett-like company takes tedious, boring work, and entrepreneurs should check whether that fits their own tastes.

principles.text: Steady growth and high profitability can cost you excitement; boredom is a real price of the Buffett model.
principles.quote: What’s the price of creating a company with good, steady revenue growth and profitability? Boredom (potenially).

principles.text: There are many valid ways to build a successful company; pick the one that fits your tastes.
principles.quote: There are a million ways to build a successful company (however success is defined as). Get big fast, like OpenAI. Grow a family dynasty over 100 years. Stay a small mom and pop business.

principles.text: Before copying Buffett's results, consider the day-to-day work required and whether you'd enjoy it.
principles.quote: But…I don’t think we think enough about the day to day work to achieve what he did and how it fits into our own tastes.

principles.text: Mastery in any field requires decades of tedious, boring work, and that boredom is acceptable.
principles.quote: I think you can argue that to be the best at anything (sports, art, etc), it requires decades of tedious, boring work.

principles.text: Even a founder who loves starting things and exciting parts of business must sometimes accept tedium to achieve greatness.
principles.quote: greatness might occasionally require accepting tedious and boring.

principles.text: A company can be exciting by nature (a newspaper) yet become boring once it prioritizes financial success under disciplined control.
principles.quote: But once it got under Buffett’s control and became more financially successful…it was much more boring.
